title: Homogeneous supported division from prescribed first exponents
statement: Let L be a field [def-weil-field], n a natural number, and iota any finite linearly ordered set. Let G:iota -> L[[T_1,...,T_n]], and let alpha_i be the first nonzero exponent of G_i in ascending total-degree lexicographic order [def-trf-formal-initial-diagram] [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Write H_i for the homogeneous component of G_i in degree |alpha_i|, viewed as a polynomial by truncation at |alpha_i|+1. For every homogeneous degree t, the indexed family T^b H_i (b in the translated first-dividing-vertex region Delta_i, |b|+|alpha_i|=t), together with the monomials of degree t outside the union of vertex orthants, is a basis: every degree-t homogeneous polynomial has unique finitely supported L-coefficients in that indexed family [def-trf-supported-homogeneous-division]. Neither monotonicity of the orthant union nor minimality or ordering of the exponents alpha_i is assumed.

source.place: BM 1997, (7.1), (7.2)(1)--(2), and Lemma 7.7; original generic-monotone-diagram step 5 (finite triangular column argument).

proof.text: Fix t. The degree-t exponent set is finite. Every exponent in the generated orthant union has a least dividing index, since iota is finite and linearly ordered. Assign it to this index and subtract alpha_i; assign exponents outside the union to the remainder. This gives a bijection from DivisionIndex to the degree-t monomials, including empty quotient regions and the empty index family.

Each initial homogeneous form H_i has degree |alpha_i|, nonzero coefficient at alpha_i, and zero coefficients at earlier exponents. Translation preserves degree-lex order, so each column T^b H_i has nonzero coefficient at its assigned exponent alpha_i+b and zero earlier coefficients. Remainder columns are the assigned monomials.

Order the finite degree-t exponent set in degree-lex order. The matrix of these columns in the monomial basis is triangular with nonzero diagonal over L, hence invertible. Its inverse supplies the unique coefficient family. Finite coefficients identify with the Finsupp coefficients in HasUniqueDivision. The argument includes t below every vertex degree and n=0.
